A universal basic income (UBI) is a regular cash payment given to every resident, regardless of employment status, income, or wealth. A very high UBI—high enough to cover not merely subsistence but a broadly comfortable standard of living—would be a much more ambitious policy than most real-world UBI proposals. Its advocates argue that, if financed through extremely progressive taxation, monetary expansion, or some combination, it could reshape the distribution of income and economic security.

1. Eliminating poverty

The most direct argument is simple: if every person receives an income above the poverty threshold, then income poverty is, by definition, greatly reduced or eliminated.

A high UBI could:

  • Guarantee that everyone can afford basic necessities such as food, housing, utilities, healthcare-related costs, and transportation.
  • Reduce reliance on conditional welfare programs that require applications, eligibility tests, work requirements, or frequent recertification.
  • Reach people who are often missed by existing assistance systems, including people with unstable work, informal employment, homelessness, caregiving responsibilities, or difficulty navigating bureaucracy.
  • Provide immediate support during personal shocks—job loss, illness, family breakdown, relocation, or unexpected expenses—without requiring people to prove hardship.

Because the payment is universal and automatic, supporters argue it avoids the “welfare cliff,” where someone loses benefits after earning slightly more income. People could take part-time work, accept temporary jobs, or start a business without risking the loss of all support.

A high UBI would not automatically solve every form of deprivation—especially if housing, healthcare, or other essential services remain scarce or expensive—but it would give households far more purchasing power and bargaining capacity.

2. Reducing economic inequality

A universal payment is equal in cash terms, but its impact is unequal in a progressive direction: a fixed payment represents a much larger share of income for poor and middle-income households than for wealthy ones.

If financed through highly progressive taxes—such as steep marginal income taxes on top earners, wealth taxes, inheritance taxes, corporate taxes, land-value taxes, or taxes on capital gains—the system would effectively transfer resources from those with the greatest economic capacity to everyone else.

Advocates see several equality-enhancing effects:

  • Higher income floor: No one would be left with zero income or extreme material insecurity.
  • Greater bargaining power for workers: People would be less forced to accept dangerous, abusive, or severely underpaid jobs merely to survive.
  • Reduced dependence on inherited advantage: A guaranteed income could partly offset disparities in family wealth, social connections, and access to education.
  • More equal access to opportunity: People could afford training, relocation, childcare, or time to search for better work.
  • Broader sharing of productivity gains: If technology and capital produce growing wealth with fewer workers, UBI could distribute some of that wealth beyond owners and shareholders.

Although wealthy individuals would also receive the nominal UBI, advocates generally regard that as administratively useful and politically stabilizing. Under a sufficiently progressive tax system, high-income people would pay far more in tax than they receive in UBI, while lower-income households would receive more than they contribute.

3. Security amid automation and technological unemployment

Automation, artificial intelligence, robotics, and digital platforms can increase productivity while reducing demand for certain kinds of labor. Even if new jobs emerge in the long run, transitions can be painful: workers may lose occupations, regions may lose industries, and retraining may be slow or inaccessible.

A high UBI is proposed as a form of social insurance against this uncertainty.

It could provide:

  • Income continuity during displacement: Workers whose jobs disappear would not immediately face eviction, hunger, or financial collapse.
  • Time for retraining or education: People could learn new skills without needing to work full-time at any available job.
  • Support for career transitions: Workers could move to new regions, enter apprenticeships, care for family members, or take time to find suitable employment.
  • Recognition of unpaid work: Caregiving, volunteering, artistic work, study, and community participation would become more financially feasible.
  • A cushion if paid work becomes less available overall: If automation permanently reduces the number of stable, well-paid jobs, UBI would decouple basic survival from continuous employment.

Supporters often frame this as a response to a deeper change: if society can produce abundant goods and services with less human labor, then access to income need not depend entirely on selling one’s labor.

4. Greater individual freedom and security

Beyond poverty and automation, advocates argue that a high UBI would expand practical freedom.

A person with guaranteed income may be better able to:

  • Leave an abusive partner or unsafe household.
  • Refuse exploitative employment.
  • Take entrepreneurial risks.
  • Pursue education or creative projects.
  • Care for children, elderly relatives, or disabled family members.
  • Participate in civic life, local organizations, or political activity.

This is sometimes described as “freedom from coercion by economic desperation.” The claim is not that people would stop working, but that work choices would become less compelled by immediate survival needs.

5. Possible macroeconomic benefits

A high UBI could also stabilize demand in the economy. Lower-income households tend to spend a larger portion of additional income than affluent households, so redistributing income downward could increase consumption of everyday goods and services.

During recessions or periods of job loss, automatic payments could act as a built-in economic stabilizer:

  • Household spending would fall less sharply.
  • Businesses would retain more customers.
  • Local economies would be less vulnerable to sudden income losses.
  • Governments might not need to design emergency aid from scratch.

If financed partly by monetary expansion in an economy with unused productive capacity, proponents argue it could increase demand without necessarily creating severe inflation. They often compare this to central-bank money creation used during crises, but directed more directly toward households rather than financial markets.

6. The financing rationale

Extremely progressive taxation

The moral and economic justification for very progressive financing is that large fortunes and high incomes often reflect access to capital, monopoly power, inheritance, natural resources, or the cumulative productivity of society—not only individual effort.

A high UBI funded by progressive taxes is therefore presented as a social dividend: the public shares in the wealth generated by institutions, infrastructure, scientific knowledge, legal systems, natural resources, and technology built across generations.

Potential revenue sources proposed by supporters include:

  • Very high top marginal income-tax rates.
  • Taxes on large fortunes or net wealth.
  • Stronger taxation of capital gains and dividends.
  • Corporate-profit taxes.
  • Inheritance and estate taxes.
  • Taxes on monopoly rents, land values, carbon emissions, or resource extraction.
  • Taxes on automation-related gains or excess profits.

Significant monetary expansion

The monetary-expansion argument rests on the idea that governments or central banks can create money, particularly when productive resources—workers, factories, housing capacity, energy infrastructure—are underused. In that situation, additional spending may increase production and employment rather than merely raise prices.

Proponents also argue that monetary creation is already used to support financial systems, banks, and asset markets. A “people’s monetary policy” would distribute newly created money more broadly through UBI instead.

However, this rationale depends heavily on real economic capacity. If the supply of housing, food, energy, healthcare, and other essentials cannot rise enough to meet increased demand, inflation could erode the real value of the UBI.

7. Important limitations and objections

A very high UBI is far more difficult to implement than a modest income guarantee. Major concerns include:

  • Cost: A payment large enough to provide a comfortable living standard for everyone would require enormous tax revenue, major spending cuts elsewhere, substantial money creation, or all three.
  • Inflation: If demand rises faster than the supply of goods and services, especially housing and healthcare, prices could rise sharply.
  • Tax avoidance and capital flight: Extremely high taxes on wealth and income could encourage avoidance, evasion, relocation, or changes in investment behavior unless coordinated internationally and enforced effectively.
  • Labor-supply effects: Some people might reduce paid work, which could be beneficial in cases of overwork or caregiving but could also reduce production and tax revenue if the effect were large.
  • Political feasibility: Wealthy individuals and firms would likely strongly oppose the taxes required.
  • Public-service tradeoffs: Cash cannot fully substitute for universal healthcare, education, housing policy, disability supports, and other public services. A UBI that replaced these services could leave some people worse off.

For these reasons, even many UBI supporters favor a moderate basic income combined with strong public services, housing construction, labor protections, and progressive taxation rather than relying exclusively on a very high cash payment.

In summary, the case for a high UBI is that a rich, technologically advanced society could guarantee everyone a secure share of its resources. Its central promised benefits are the elimination of income poverty, a major compression of inequality, and protection against the insecurity created by automation and unstable labor markets. Its central challenge is ensuring that financing and supply capacity are strong enough that the policy raises real living standards rather than producing unaffordable fiscal burdens or inflation.

The Case for a High-Level Universal Basic Income: A Radical but Necessary Solution to Poverty, Inequality, and Automation

Introduction

The 21st century has ushered in an era of unprecedented technological advancement, yet it has also deepened economic inequality and precarity for the majority of the global population. Automation, artificial intelligence, and algorithmic optimization are rapidly displacing jobs, while the ultra-wealthy hoard ever-greater shares of wealth. Traditional welfare systems, labor protections, and economic policies have failed to keep pace with these transformations, leaving millions in poverty and millions more just one crisis away from destitution. The solution to this crisis is not incremental reform but a radical restructuring of economic policy: a high-level universal basic income (UBI), funded through extreme wealth redistribution and monetary expansion. Only such a measure can eradicate poverty, reduce inequality, and provide a safety net in an economy increasingly dominated by automation.

This essay argues that a high-level UBI—funded by 90%+ wealth taxes on the ultra-wealthy and large-scale monetary expansion—is not just desirable but necessary to address the structural failures of capitalism in the digital age. Such a policy would not only guarantee a dignified standard of living for all but also stimulate economic growth, reduce systemic inequality, and prepare society for the inevitable job displacement caused by technological progress.

The Failure of Existing Welfare Systems and the Need for a Radical Alternative

Current welfare systems—whether in the form of means-tested benefits, unemployment insurance, or social safety nets—are fractured, bureaucratic, and inadequate in the face of modern economic challenges. They create perverse incentives, exclude the most vulnerable, and fail to address the root causes of poverty: structural unemployment, stagnant wages, and wealth concentration.

  1. Means-Testing Creates Barriers and Stigma – Most welfare programs require proof of need, leading to long application processes, eligibility denials, and the stigma of "dependency." This discourages work and punishes those who are temporarily unemployed or underemployed.
  2. Automation Displaces Workers Without Alternatives – Robots, AI, and algorithmic management are replacing jobs at an accelerating rate. According to the World Economic Forum, by 2025, 85 million jobs may be displaced by automation, while only 97 million new roles may emerge. Without a guaranteed income floor, millions will be left with no means of subsistence.
  3. Wealth Inequality is at Historic Highs – The top 1% own more than half the global wealth, while the bottom 50% hold less than 1% (Credit Suisse Global Wealth Report, 2023). Traditional taxation (income, corporate, VAT) fails to address this imbalance because the ultra-wealthy shift income into capital gains, trusts, and offshore accounts, evading progressive taxation.

A universal basic income (UBI), in contrast, provides unconditional cash payments to all citizens, eliminating bureaucratic hurdles, reducing poverty, and allowing individuals the freedom to pursue education, entrepreneurship, or care work without financial desperation.

Why a High-Level UBI? The Case for Generous Funding

While many UBI proposals suggest modest amounts (e.g., $1,000–$2,000 per month), eradication of poverty and true economic security require a far higher baseline—one that ensures no one lives in material hardship. Research from Finland’s UBI experiment (2017–2018) and Kenya’s GiveDirectly pilot shows that even modest UBI can improve mental health, employment rates, and economic resilience. However, true poverty eradication demands a UBI that covers basic needs without forcing recipients into exploitative work.

What Constitutes a "High-Level" UBI?

A high-level UBI should be sufficient to:

  • Cover housing (rent or mortgage payments)
  • Provide food security (enough for a healthy diet)
  • Allow for healthcare access (including mental health support)
  • Enable education and skill development
  • Permit leisure and cultural participation

For a single adult in the U.S., this would likely require at least $2,500–$3,500 per month (or $30,000–$42,000 annually), adjusted for cost of living. For a family of four, it could range from $50,000–$70,000 annually. Such a figure ensures no one is forced into poverty by economic shifts—whether automation, inflation, or job loss.

Funding the UBI: Extreme Redistribution and Monetary Expansion

The primary objection to UBI is always: "How will we pay for it?" The answer lies in two radical but necessary fiscal policies:

  1. A 90%+ Wealth Tax on the Ultra-Wealthy
  2. Large-Scale Monetary Expansion (Modern Monetary Theory - MMT)

1. A 90%+ Wealth Tax on the Top 0.1%

The top 0.1% of households (those with $20+ million in net worth) currently pay far too little in taxes relative to their wealth accumulation. A 90% marginal tax rate on wealth above $50 million (as proposed by economists like Gabriel Zucman) would:

  • Raise trillions annually (Zucman estimates $2.5–$3 trillion per year in the U.S. alone).
  • Disincentivize hoarding wealth while still allowing entrepreneurs to retain a portion of their earnings.
  • Reduce dynastic wealth accumulation, preventing the concentration of power in the hands of a few families.

Countries like France and Spain have experimented with wealth taxes, but they are too low (1–2%) to make a significant dent in inequality. A 90%+ rate on the top 0.1% would radically alter the economic landscape, ensuring that those who benefit most from the economy contribute the most.

2. Monetary Expansion via Modern Monetary Theory (MMT)

Since the ultra-wealthy can avoid taxes, and public debt is not inherently inflationary (as MMT argues), governments can print money to fund UBI without causing hyperinflation—if managed responsibly.

  • Japan and the U.S. have run large fiscal deficits for decades without hyperinflation, proving that debt is not inherently destabilizing when the currency is the world’s reserve.
  • Helicopter money (direct cash transfers funded by central banks) has been successfully tested in Switzerland (2020) and Japan (2021) to combat deflation.
  • Inflation can be controlled through price controls, land value taxes, and progressive taxation, ensuring that the burden does not fall on the poor.

By combining wealth taxes with monetary expansion, we can fund a high UBI without relying on regressive consumption taxes (VAT, sales taxes) that hurt the poor.

The Economic and Social Benefits of a High-Level UBI

1. Eradication of Poverty

  • Absolute poverty (living on less than $2.15/day) could be eliminated globally with sufficient UBI funding.
  • Relative poverty (living below 60% of median income) would be drastically reduced, as seen in Alaska’s Permanent Fund Dividend (PFD), where residents receive $1,000–$2,000 annually, improving health and education outcomes.

2. Reduction of Inequality

  • Wealth inequality would shrink as the ultra-rich are forced to contribute more.
  • Income inequality would decrease as everyone receives a floor of economic security, preventing the bottom 90% from being exploited by the top 1%.

3. Preparation for Automation and the Gig Economy

  • Workers displaced by AI would have financial security to retrain or pursue new careers.
  • Gig workers, freelancers, and the self-employed would no longer face financial instability due to irregular income.
  • Care work, art, and community-building—currently undervalued—would be more accessible, as people are not forced into exploitative jobs.

4. Economic Stimulus and Innovation

  • People with financial security spend more, stimulating local economies.
  • Entrepreneurship increases when people are not desperate for survival.
  • Reduced stress and better health lead to higher productivity in the workforce.

5. Simplification of the Welfare State

  • Ends bureaucratic red tape—no more eligibility checks, asset tests, or humiliating applications.
  • Reduces stigma—people are not seen as "lazy" if they receive support.
  • Lowers administrative costs—studies show UBI is cheaper to administer than traditional welfare.

Counterarguments and Rebuttals

1. "It’s Too Expensive!"

  • The U.S. spends $1.5 trillion annually on welfare programs—a UBI could be more efficient and more effective.
  • The wealthiest 0.1% could fund it entirely—if they are willing to pay their fair share.
  • Monetary expansion is not inflationary if managed properly—Japan and the U.S. prove this.

2. "People Won’t Work!"

  • Studies show UBI increases employment—people work more when they have security (e.g., Finland’s UBI experiment found no drop in employment).
  • Many jobs are already automated—UBI prepares society for this reality.
  • Humans need purpose beyond work—UBI allows for art, education, and community engagement.

3. "It’s Unfair to Tax the Rich More!"

  • The rich are already benefiting disproportionately from the economy—why shouldn’t they pay more?
  • Wealth taxes are progressive—they take a larger share from those who have the most.
  • Without redistribution, inequality will only worsen, leading to social unrest and political instability.

Conclusion: A UBI is Not Just Desirable—It’s Necessary for Survival

The 21st century is defined by two contradictory trends:

  1. Technological progress that could eliminate scarcity.
  2. Economic inequality that traps millions in poverty.

The only solution that addresses both is a high-level universal basic income, funded by extreme wealth redistribution and monetary expansion. Such a policy would: ✅ Eradicate poverty by guaranteeing a dignified standard of living. ✅ Reduce inequality by forcing the ultra-wealthy to contribute. ✅ Prepare society for automation by providing financial security. ✅ Simplify and improve welfare systems by eliminating bureaucracy. ✅ Stimulate economic growth by putting money in the hands of consumers.

The alternative—doing nothing—is economic suicide. The ultra-wealthy, corporate elites, and technocrats who resist UBI do so not out of economic necessity, but out of self-interest. A society that can produce abundance but tolerates destitution is not merely inefficient—it is unjust. Universal basic income at a very high level, guaranteed to every resident as a right, is the cleanest, most powerful way to abolish poverty, reduce inequality, and stabilize an economy upended by automation. The scale of this project should match the scale of the problem. That means funding UBI with extreme progressive mechanisms—90%+ marginal taxes on extreme concentrations of wealth, robust inheritance taxes at the very top, resource and land rents, and, where appropriate, large-scale monetary expansion directed to households. This is not a utopian dream; it is a realistic, necessary rebalancing of the social contract in an era when productive capacity increasingly derives from capital, code, and collective knowledge rather than from human labor alone.

Start with first principles. Income is not only a means to buy goods; it is the foundation of freedom. Without a secure floor, choice is a fiction and “market participation” a euphemism for coercion. A universal, unconditional income restores genuine bargaining power to individuals: the power to refuse exploitation, to leave abusive workplaces, to invest in education, care work, or entrepreneurship, and to participate in civic life without fear of immediate ruin. Targeted programs try to do this through bureaucratic filters that are expensive, stigmatizing, and riddled with gaps. A high-level UBI does it directly, efficiently, and with dignity.

Morally, UBI recognizes that much of what we call “private wealth” is built on public goods. Property rights, contract enforcement, the legal system, the patent regime, the internet, basic science, and the cumulative know-how of generations are social creations. The extraordinary fortunes at the top rest on this common inheritance. A steep wealth tax and large inheritance tax above very high thresholds do not confiscate legitimate effort; they recycle windfalls that owe more to network effects, monopoly power, preferential access, and path dependence than to individual merit. The public has a rightful claim on the returns to the commons.

Economically, a high UBI is not a handout; it is infrastructure. Cash transfers are among the most empirically validated anti-poverty tools in the world. Experiments from Alaska’s dividend to Finland’s basic income pilot, from Canadian negative-income-tax trials to U.S. guaranteed-income programs and large-scale transfers during the pandemic, consistently show reductions in poverty and stress, improvements in health, education, and crime outcomes, and no mass withdrawal from work. When labor supply responses appear, they are modest and often reflect beneficial choices—more schooling, caregiving, entrepreneurship, and better job matching. A substantial UBI would act as an automatic stabilizer: when downturns hit, household budgets hold up; when the economy overheats, the program can be calibrated to macro conditions. It simplifies a sprawling welfare state, slashes administrative costs, and reduces the poverty trap created by means-tested phaseouts.

Automation makes UBI not only desirable but urgent. The productive frontier is shifting from human labor to capital-intensive systems—robots, AI, and software with negligible marginal cost. The result is a decoupling of productivity from wages and a concentration of income in owners of capital and dominant platforms. Attempting to “retrain” our way out of this dynamic is a losing strategy when machines rapidly outpace human performance across tasks. We must delink basic security from wage labor. A high-level UBI ensures that gains from automation are socialized and widely shared, turning technological progress into a dividend rather than a threat.

This can include exit taxes, comprehensive information reporting, strong penalties for evasion, global coordination, and withholding at source on domestic financial assets. Even a one-time levy on billionaire wealth would raise sums sufficient to finance a generous UBI for a year; an ongoing, steep progressive wealth tax, combined with high top-bracket income and capital gains rates, can sustain a large portion of the program thereafter.

  • A 90% inheritance tax on bequests above very large exemptions (tens of millions), preventing the ossification of dynasties that choke mobility and democracy. Intergenerational fortunes are the purest form of unearned windfall; recycling them into a universal dividend is fair and economically healthy.

  • Resource and land value taxes. Land and natural resources are pure economic rents generated by location, scarcity, and public investment. Capturing these rents at scale is efficient (they don’t distort productive activity) and just (they arise from common endowments). Carbon fees and spectrum royalties should flow directly into the UBI.

  • A modest financial-transaction tax and stronger minimum corporate taxes with global coordination. These reduce unproductive churn and profit shifting while contributing revenue.

  • Large-scale monetary expansion directed to households—“people’s QE”—especially during periods of slack or deflationary pressure from automation-driven cost declines. A central bank can deliver UBI directly via digital accounts, adjusting the net fiscal impulse to meet inflation and employment targets. Unlike asset purchases that inflate markets and enrich a narrow elite, direct transfers stimulate demand broadly, which is both fairer and more effective.

The standard objections—“inflation,” “capital flight,” “people will stop working”—do not withstand scrutiny when addressed with competent design.

Inflation is about the balance of demand and supply. If UBI is funded primarily by shifting buying power from those with the highest savings rates to those who spend locally, the net demand effect is positive but manageable. Automation and global capacity expansions are deflationary forces that make room for higher household incomes without runaway prices. Additionally, monetary-financed tranches can be countercyclical: increase when unemployment rises and taper when inflation nears target, using the UBI itself as a macro tool. Where bottlenecks exist—housing, healthcare, childcare—the solution is not to keep people poor but to expand supply through investment, competition policy, faster permitting, and public options. Indexing UBI to prices protects purchasing power if inflation does tick up.

Capital flight is a political choice, not a law of nature. Strong enforcement, global reporting standards, sanctions for tax havens, exit taxes for those who move capital abroad, and withholding on domestic assets are practical. The largest markets have leverage; they can set the terms of access. Crucially, investing wealth in stable, prosperous societies with robust consumer demand is attractive even to the wealthy. A healthier, more equal economy is safer and more dynamic, which is good for business as a whole.

Work disincentives are mischaracterized. A high UBI strengthens workers’ bargaining power and raises the floor under low-wage jobs. If some undesirable jobs require higher pay or better conditions, that is a feature, not a bug—it accelerates productivity-enhancing automation and pushes firms to share gains more fairly. Evidence from cash programs shows limited reductions in labor supply overall, with larger benefits in mental health, entrepreneurship, and educational attainment. The long-term effects—more human capital, less stress, less crime—are growth-friendly.

Politically, universality is a virtue. Programs reserved for the poor are often poor programs, vulnerable to stigma and cuts. A universal dividend builds durable coalitions because everyone has a stake. It also lowers administrative friction: no means tests, no asset tests, no Kafkaesque compliance. Deliver it monthly, automatically, through a public payments system. Replace or consolidate a web of less effective subsidies and tax expenditures, while preserving or enhancing services that markets undersupply (healthcare, disability support, housing for the unhoused). Clarity and simplicity win trust.

Critics will say this agenda is too radical. Radical is accepting mass precarity in the face of unprecedented productive capacity. Radical is transferring trillions in central bank interventions to financial markets while balking at direct support for people. Radical is letting democracy decay under the weight of inequality and oligarchic power. A high-level UBI funded by extreme progressive mechanisms is, in truth, pragmatic: it aligns incentives, reduces administrative waste, stabilizes demand, and inoculates society against the shocks of technological change.

The deeper question is what kind of freedom we believe in. If freedom means only the right to compete without a net, then freedom belongs to the lucky and the already-secure. If freedom means the real capacity to plan a life—to leave a bad job, to care for a child or an aging parent, to start a business, to learn, to create, to refuse exploitation—then a robust, universal income is the shortest path to it. We have the wealth. We have the technology. We lack only the decision to treat security not as a privilege granted by employers or markets, but as a birthright in a civilized society.

The promise of automation is a world where necessities are cheap, knowledge is abundant, and human time is liberated. Without a universal basic income at scale, that promise curdles into anxiety and exclusion. With it, we can turn productivity into prosperity for all. That is not merely an economic program; it is the foundation for a freer, fairer, and more resilient democracy.

    • Fairness and reciprocity: Those capturing outsized gains from globalization, market power, and automation contribute more to a social dividend that benefits all.

Friends, neighbors, fellow citizens—

We stand at the edge of a great turning. For two centuries, the promise of progress has been that machines would liberate human beings—liberate us from drudgery, from scarcity, from the cruel lottery of birth. And yet today, too many work more and have less. Too many live one bill, one illness, one layoff away from crisis. The engines of prosperity that our grandparents built now kick up more dust than rain for ordinary people. The productivity of a million miracles flows past us into reservoirs we can see but never touch.

It does not have to be this way.

I am here to argue for a very high universal basic income—an income large enough to guarantee a dignified life, not bare survival. A basic income that says, with absolute clarity: in a rich society, no one will be hungry, unhoused, or humiliated by the fear of falling. A basic income that is unconditional, universal, and permanent. Funded boldly and honestly—by taxing extreme concentrations of wealth that were built by all of us, and by channeling the power of money creation to people rather than just to markets. A basic income that turns technological progress into human freedom.

Some will say this is utopian. I say it is overdue.

First, let us be clear about the moral claim. Wealth is not merely the product of individual genius; it is the harvest of generations—of public schools and roads, of shared knowledge, of science built in public universities, of care work and community bonds that never appear on a balance sheet. Every great fortune stands on foundations poured by the many. A high universal basic income is a dividend from that common inheritance. It is a way of paying ourselves for the ancestors we share and the future we will build.

Second, let us talk about the world we are walking into. Automation, artificial intelligence, and platform monopolies are not on the horizon—they are here. They are amplifying the output of those who own them and displacing the bargaining power of those who do not. We are told to retrain, to hustle harder, to become more “resilient.” But resilience without security is just a new word for anxiety. The truth is that technology magnifies existing rules of distribution. If we change nothing, more power will tilt toward capital and fewer people will have the stability to plan a life. With a high UBI, we do not fear the robot—we welcome it. We turn every innovation into a pathway to more free time, more creativity, more care for each other. We convert technological displacement into technological dividends.

Third, the economics. We are already rich enough. The issue is not whether we can afford a high basic income; it is whether we can afford the cost of not having one—lost potential, chronic stress, preventable illness, crime born of desperation, and an economy trapped in low-demand, low-trust cycles. Cash transfers are one of the most studied, effective tools we have for reducing poverty and improving outcomes. Time and again, when people have a floor, they use it to stand taller—starting businesses, seeking better jobs, caring for family, learning new skills. Freedom is efficient.

How do we pay for it? Two powerful tools:

  • Radical wealth taxation. Not tinkering at the edges—real, structural rebalancing. A progressive tax on extreme net worth above very high thresholds. Closing loopholes, ending the secrecy that lets fortunes invisibly compound beyond any social accountability, aligning capital gains and inheritance taxes with the value created by our shared systems. This is not punishment; it is reciprocity. A society that protects property and stabilizes markets has the right to collect a dividend from the fortunes it makes possible. Today, wealth compounds faster than wages. A wealth tax helps rebalance that dynamic and funds a universal guarantee that strengthens the very markets the wealthy depend on—by ensuring consumers have money in their pockets and workers have the power to say yes or no.

  • Large-scale monetary expansion as a people’s dividend. For years, when crises hit, we have created new money to preserve balance sheets and asset prices. We call it “quantitative easing,” and most of it circulates in financial markets. What if, instead, the new money entered through the hands of the people—equally, automatically, predictably? Think of it as democratizing seigniorage: if we can create money to save banks, we can create money to save families. Will some worry about inflation? Of course—and we should treat that worry with seriousness. But inflation is not magic; it is about real resources. We can design this dividend with automatic stabilizers—taxes that dial up at the top when demand runs hot, and investments that expand productive capacity: housing, energy, health care, childcare, broadband. We can pair a people’s dividend with anti-monopoly enforcement and price-gouging protections so new money doesn’t simply chase old bottlenecks. The point is not reckless printing; it is responsible, transparent public money creation that benefits everyone, not just the already wealthy.

These tools are complementary. Wealth taxes help prevent runaway inequality and pull excess purchasing power from the top, easing inflation pressures. A universal dividend delivers spending power to the base, stabilizing demand and giving people genuine bargaining power. Together, they form a flywheel of shared prosperity.

Now, let us answer the familiar objections.

“People won’t work.” The evidence is plain: when people have security, they make better choices. Most continue to work; some work less because they go back to school, care for family, or leave abusive jobs. That is not laziness; that is freedom. Work without desperation is better work. Firms compete for talent rather than people competing for permission to live.

“It’s too expensive.” Poverty is what’s expensive. Emergency rooms as primary care are expensive. Police as social workers are expensive. Prisons as housing policy are expensive. The bureaucracy of means-testing is expensive. A universal benefit replaces layers of administrative waste with trust. And the money exists—it is just locked at the top or trapped in financial loops. We will unlock it.

“It will cause inflation.” Inflation is not a single dial; it is a tapestry of supply constraints, market power, and expectations. A well-designed UBI recognizes this. We expand housing supply, modernize the grid, invest in domestic production where it matters, and tax back excess demand at the top when needed. The alternative is what we already do: pump trillions into asset markets and then pretend that asset price inflation is not inflation at all.

“What about the people who don’t deserve it?” Everyone deserves dignity. That is the point of universal programs: they are simpler, more trusted, less divisive. We stop turning neighbors into caseworkers and coroners. We build solidarity, not suspicion.

A high universal basic income is not just an economic policy. It is a peace treaty with the future. It says to our children: you will not inherit a race to the bottom. You will inherit time to think and room to breathe. Start a company or start a band. Care for a parent or raise a child. Learn a trade or write a book. Say yes because you want to, and say no because you can. That is what prosperity is supposed to feel like.

And let us be clear: this is not charity. It is justice. The richest among us did not build their empires alone; they built on public goods, public order, and public faith. It is time to return a portion of that compounded benefit to the public. And money creation should not be a private spigot for the already secure; it should be a public tool that serves public ends.

We will need courage. Courage to see through the fog of “that’s how it’s always been.” Courage to take on special interests and dismantle the opacity that hides fortunes from accountability. Courage to try something as old as a community and as new as the frontier: that everyone counts, and that our shared wealth should be used to guarantee each person a life worthy of a human being.

Imagine the day the first universal payment lands. Overnight, millions exhale. Evictions avoided. Groceries bought without dread. Entrepreneurs file LLCs. Volunteers flood civic life. Artists make art. Students study what matters. Caregivers are valued. The bottom becomes a floor, not a trap. The economy shifts from fear to possibility.

We can do this. We have the tools. We have the need. We have the moral claim.

So let us be bold. Let us enact a very high universal basic income and fund it with the honesty this moment demands: by taxing extreme wealth and by using our power to create money for human flourishing rather than financial alchemy. Let us say, together, that in our society, no one is disposable; no one is a rounding error; no one is left behind.

The future will judge us not by our caution but by our courage. Let’s build the world where freedom is not a slogan but a budget line. Let’s build the world where technology liberates rather than terrifies. Let’s build the world where the dividends of progress reach every kitchen table.

This is our generation’s chance to keep the promise of progress. Let’s take it.

A UBI set above the poverty line guarantees that every individual and family can meet their essential needs. Financing a high UBI through extremely progressive taxation (e.g., a marginal tax rate of 70% on top incomes, a substantial wealth tax) redistributes resources from the richest to the broader population.   • Economic stimulus: Because recipients are likely to spend the additional income immediately on goods and services, a high UBI boosts aggregate demand, supporting local businesses and potentially creating new jobs.

By guaranteeing a dignified existence, it not only addresses immediate material needs but also unlocks human potential, fosters social cohesion, and paves the way for a more equitable and adaptable economy. Core Concept: A "Very High" UBI

A "very high" UBI, often proposed at or near the official poverty line (e.g., ~$1,200/month per adult in the U.S.), is fundamentally different from a modest supplemental income. It is designed to be a liveable floor—an income sufficient to cover basic necessities like housing, food, and healthcare without any other earnings.

This ambitious policy is typically paired with one of two radical financing mechanisms:

Reasons and Supposed Benefits

1. Eliminate Poverty Absolutely and Unconditionally

  • Reason: Traditional welfare systems are conditional, complex, and stigmatizing. They create "benefit cliffs" where earning more money can result in a loss of benefits, trapping people in poverty. A very high UBI is universal and unconditional.
  • Supposed Benefits:
    • Absolute Elimination: By providing an income above the poverty line to every citizen, poverty, by definition, is eradicated. No one would lack the basic means for survival.

    • No More Benefit Cliffs: Since the UBI is not reduced as earnings increase, it always pays to work additional hours, removing a major disincentive to work that exists in current systems.

2. Dramatically Reduce Economic Inequality

  • Reason: Extreme wealth and income inequality are seen as destabilizing forces for democracy and society. They concentrate power and opportunity in the hands of a few.

    • Wealth De-Concentration: Taxes on wealth (e.g., a net worth tax) directly target accumulated capital, preventing dynastic wealth and ensuring capital circulates through the broader economy.
    • Bargaining Power Shift: With a guaranteed safety net, workers have far more power to refuse exploitative wages and poor working conditions. This forces employers to offer better pay and benefits, reducing the inequality between capital owners and laborers.

  • Reason: Advances in AI and robotics threaten to disrupt a vast number of jobs, not just in manufacturing but also in white-collar sectors (e.g., truck driving, retail, analysis, and even some creative fields). This could lead to structural, permanent unemployment.
  • Supposed Benefits:

    • Encouraging Adaptation: It provides people with the financial security to retrain, go back to school, start a business, or pursue creative and caregiving roles that are less likely to be automated but are currently undervalued by the market.

A. Extremely Progressive Taxation

B. Significant Monetary Expansion ("Modern Monetary Theory" Approach)

  • Rationale: Proponents of Modern Monetary Theory (MMT) argue that a sovereign currency issuer (like the U.S. government) cannot run out of money. The real limit is inflation, not budget deficits. Its appeal lies in its simplicity, its power to address multiple systemic problems at once, and its potential to serve as a foundation for a more humane and equitable future economy. Introduction

The modern economy is plagued by deepening inequality, persistent poverty, and the looming threat of automation-driven unemployment. The Failures of the Current System

1. Persistent Poverty Despite Economic Growth

Despite decades of economic expansion, poverty remains entrenched. In the United States, 40% of Americans cannot afford a $400 emergency expense, while 40 million people live in poverty. Traditional welfare programs are stigmatizing, means-tested, and inefficient, often trapping people in bureaucratic nightmares. UBI eliminates these inefficiencies by providing direct, unconditional cash transfers, ensuring that no one falls through the cracks.

The richest 1% own more wealth than the bottom 90% combined. Billionaires like Jeff Bezos and Elon Musk accumulate wealth at unprecedented rates while workers struggle with stagnant wages. A 90%+ wealth tax on the ultra-rich would not only fund UBI but also correct the grotesque imbalance that has emerged from decades of neoliberal policies.

3. The Automation Crisis

AI and robotics are eliminating jobs faster than new ones are created. Self-checkout kiosks, automated factories, and AI-driven services threaten millions of jobs. Without intervention, we face a future of mass unemployment and social unrest. UBI provides a financial safety net, allowing people to retrain, pursue creative work, or simply live with dignity.

Why UBI Is the Solution

1. Eradicating Poverty Immediately

Unlike welfare programs that require complex eligibility checks, UBI is universal and unconditional. Every citizen receives the same amount, ensuring that no one is left behind. Studies from pilot programs in Finland, Kenya, and Stockton, California show that UBI reduces poverty, improves mental health, and increases economic security.

2. Reducing Inequality Through Extreme Redistribution

The ultra-wealthy have hoarded trillions in offshore accounts and tax havens. A 90%+ wealth tax on fortunes over $100 million would generate trillions annually—enough to fund a generous UBI without raising taxes on the middle class. 3. Preparing for the Post-Work Economy

As automation accelerates, traditional employment models will collapse. UBI decouples survival from labor, allowing people to:

  • Pursue education and retraining
  • Engage in care work (parenting, eldercare, community service)
  • Start businesses or creative ventures This shift would unleash human potential rather than forcing people into precarious gig economy jobs.

Counterarguments and Rebuttals

"UBI is too expensive!"

The cost is offset by extreme wealth taxes and monetary expansion. The top 0.1% hold $15 trillion in wealth—taxing this at 90% would generate $1.5 trillion annually, enough for a $1,000/month UBI for all Americans. The Automation Revolution Demands Preparation

We are witnessing the most rapid technological transformation in human history. Artificial intelligence, robotics, and machine learning are displacing workers across every sector—from manufacturing and transportation to healthcare and professional services. While technologists debate timelines, the direction is unmistakable: millions of jobs will vanish within decades, potentially leaving entire communities economically devastated.

Traditional responses to technological unemployment—retraining programs, unemployment insurance, job creation schemes—have proven inadequate. They treat symptoms rather than causes and fail to address the fundamental reality that work itself is becoming obsolete as an economic necessity. UBI provides a proactive solution, ensuring that as machines take over productive labor, humans are not left behind but instead freed to pursue meaningful activities that define our humanity.

Eradicating Poverty Through Direct Empowerment

Poverty persists not due to lack of resources, but due to poor distribution of existing wealth. The world's richest 1% now possess more than twice the wealth of 4.5 billion people combined. A robust UBI program would directly address this imbalance by providing every citizen with unconditional financial security.

Unlike means-tested welfare programs that create poverty traps and bureaucratic barriers, UBI empowers individuals with choice and dignity. When people receive money without conditions, they invest in education, start businesses, care for family members, and contribute to their communities in ways that bureaucratic oversight cannot predict or measure. Extreme Wealth Redistribution: Justice Over Charity

The astronomical wealth accumulated by tech billionaires, hedge fund managers, and corporate dynasties represents not individual achievement but systemic capture of public resources. These fortunes were built on infrastructure funded by taxpayers, legal protections enforced by governments, and markets created through collective human knowledge and effort.

A 90%+ wealth tax on ultra-millionaires isn't confiscation—it's restitution. It recognizes that extreme wealth concentration undermines democracy, distorts markets, and perpetuates inequality. Large-scale monetary expansion, often vilified by conservatives, becomes a tool for public good when directed toward UBI rather than bank bailouts or military spending. The Federal Reserve created trillions during financial crises; imagine if those resources had been distributed directly to citizens instead of propping up failing institutions.

Economic Stimulus and Social Transformation

UBI functions as the most powerful economic stimulus possible. Unlike government spending on weapons or infrastructure that may not reach local communities effectively, direct cash transfers put purchasing power directly into people's hands. This increased demand stimulates economic activity, creates jobs, and generates tax revenue that can fund further social investments.

Beyond economics, UBI enables profound social transformation. It reduces crime by addressing root causes of desperation. It improves health outcomes by eliminating stress associated with financial insecurity. It strengthens democracy by reducing corporate influence over desperate workers. It fosters creativity and innovation by providing the security necessary for risk-taking and experimentation.

Critics argue that UBI is unaffordable, but this ignores both the massive wealth already concentrated in society and the economic costs of poverty itself. The U.S. spends over $1 trillion annually on means-tested welfare programs with complex administrative overhead. A streamlined UBI system could achieve better outcomes at lower cost.

Concerns about work disincentives ignore human nature and empirical evidence. People seek purpose, connection, and contribution—not just survival. UBI doesn't eliminate work; it eliminates exploitative work and enables people to pursue meaningful contributions to society.

Inflation fears assume that injecting money into the economy necessarily devalues currency. However, when money flows to those who spend it immediately on necessities rather than accumulating as financial assets, it stimulates productive capacity rather than speculative bubbles.

Implementing UBI requires political courage and public mobilization. The ultra-wealthy will resist redistribution efforts, and establishment politicians dependent on their support will obstruct progress. However, growing inequality, climate change, and technological disruption create windows for transformative change.

We must advocate for policies that treat UBI not as a handout but as recognition of our shared ownership of technological progress and natural resources. Funding mechanisms should include:

  • Progressive wealth taxes targeting extreme concentrations of capital
  • Carbon taxes reflecting environmental costs
  • Financial transaction taxes on speculative trading
  • Sovereign control over monetary creation
  • Public ownership of strategic industries and resources

The choice is clear: we can maintain a system that concentrates wealth among elites while billions struggle for basic necessities, or we can build an economy that serves human flourishing. The technology exists to make this vision real; what we lack is the collective will to demand it.

Our future depends not on preserving outdated economic models but on embracing bold solutions that reflect our highest values. The Only Cure for an Age of Plenty: A Radical UBI Funded by the Ultra-Wealthy

We are living in an age of staggering plenty. The world now produces enough food to feed every human being, enough housing to shelter every family, and enough medical knowledge to save countless lives. Yet poverty persists, inequality has grotesquely metastasized, and automation is quietly extinguishing the futures of millions. This is not a failure of resources; it is a failure of distribution. A universal basic income—set at a genuinely high level and funded through the most aggressive redistributive mechanisms available—is not merely a pleasant idea. It is the only coherent response to the crises facing us. And it must be funded by taking, directly and unapologetically, from the ultra-wealthy.

First, let us be clear: modest UBI proposals are a rerun of austerity in progressive clothing. A $500-a-month stipend does not eradicate poverty; it cushions it. It gives the poor just enough to remain poor without revolting. A high-level UBI, by contrast, means an unconditional income sufficient to meet the full costs of living: food, housing, utilities, healthcare, and a dignified social existence. Anything less is a bribe, not an emancipation. Anything less leaves millions at the mercy of landlords, employers, and pharmaceutical boards. A truly high-level UBI is the floor on which a society can stand with its head raised. It is not a handout; it is a dividend from the collective inheritance of centuries.

The urgency of this demand cannot be overstated. Automation and artificial intelligence are not coming; they are already here. Driverless vehicles are replacing millions of transportation workers. Chatbots are displacing customer-service agents. Algorithms are writing code, drafting legal documents, and diagnosing illnesses. Every productivity gain from this new industrial revolution flows directly into the bank accounts of shareholders and technology oligarchs. Meanwhile, the worker—once told to “just retrain” or “learn to code”—is told to compete with a machine that works for free. The game is rigged. No amount of education, grit, or “skill-building” can overcome the fundamental truth that a society no longer needs every adult’s labor. When work disappears, income must be decoupled from labor, or poverty becomes a permanent condition. A high-level UBI is the only honest acknowledgment of this technological reality.

But where, the naysayers shriek, will the money come from? The answer is obvious and requires no exotic financial engineering: take it from those who have shamelessly accumulated more than any human being could ever need. The ultra-wealthy—those whose net worths are measured in hundreds of billions—did not build their fortunes in a vacuum. They built them using roads, schools, courts, patents, and a stable society paid for by generations of working people. Their wealth is a social product, and it must be socially reclaimed. A 90% annual wealth tax on fortunes above, say, one billion dollars is not theft; it is the overdue recapture of unearned surplus. It is profoundly conservative in the best sense: it preserves the possibility of a functioning civilization instead of allowing one thousand oligarchs to hollow it out.

Do not pretend such taxes are impossible. The United States imposed a top marginal income tax rate of 91% during the postwar period, and the economy boomed. The middle class expanded. Innovation flourished. Why? Because when grotesque concentrations of wealth are broken up, demand grows from the bottom upward, and entrepreneurs find customers, not enemies. A wealth tax on the ultra-rich would not “kill innovation”; it would kill the sterile, unproductive hoarding of capital in offshore accounts, private islands, and trust funds. The only thing it would kill is the illusion that billionaires are job creators rather than job hoarders.

Those who squirm at the phrase “extreme redistribution” should sit with that discomfort and examine it. What is more extreme than a child going hungry in a country with overflowing warehouses? What is more extreme than a nurse forced to choose between buying insulin and paying rent in an economy that has no room for her sacrifice? We are told to be reasonable, moderate, and gradual while the poor die quietly and the rich purchase senators. The time for moderation is over. If funding a high-level UBI requires a confiscatory wealth tax, then let it be confiscatory. Wealth is not sacred; human dignity is.

Equally important, we must expand the imagination about money itself. In addition to taxing inherited and accumulated fortunes, we can and should fund a high-level UBI through large-scale monetary expansion—in plain language, by creating money and putting it into the hands of ordinary people instead of banks and bondholders. The trillion-dollar objections are rhetorical fear, not economic law. Every major economy has already printed trillions to bail out banks, rescue airlines, and fund endless wars. The money appears whenever it is needed for emergencies. Why is it never available for the single most important emergency: the largest disruption of labor since the Industrial Revolution?

A monetarily financed UBI would put purchasing power directly into the hands of those who will spend it: families, students, retirees, artists, and struggling workers. It would circulate through local economies, multiplying through every shop, café, and clinic. Inflation, the eternal bogeyman, can be managed through progressive taxation and public investment in housing, healthcare, and energy. The hoarded billions of the ultra-rich are already a form of inflation: they inflate asset prices, drive up rents, and distort politics. Injecting money into the bottom of the income distribution would not create bubbles; it would repair the devastated base of our economy. We do not lack money. We lack the political will to monetize human dignity instead of corporate profit.

Against every argument for a high-level UBI, the critics raise the same tired chorus: “Won’t people just stop working?” This question is a confession of how deeply we have been poisoned by the work ethic of an age that no longer exists. When people are given a secure income, history and evidence show that they do not collapse into idleness. They start businesses, care for aging parents, raise children, create art, return to school, and say no to abusive employers. The fact that someone would continue working even without fear of starvation is not a bug; it is the foundation of real freedom. And for the genuinely tedious jobs that remain—the warehouses and fast-food counters—automation can do them. If the machines are truly taking our jobs, then let them take the dull ones. We will be busy living.

Some will say that a 90% wealth tax will trigger capital flight. Let it. Let the ultra-rich flee to their tax havens and luxury bunkers. The rest of us will form international agreements, punitive exit taxes, and automatic exchange of bank information to reclaim what was always collectively produced. No law is perfectly enforced, but that does not mean we should abandon the law. The alternative—keeping poverty alive because the rich have the means to escape taxation—is a moral failure dressed in realism.

We must also understand that this is not only an economic argument; it is a moral demand. A society that has enough for everyone and chooses to let millions live in precarity is not a society; it is a machine for generating misery. Extreme inequality is not a natural disaster. It is a policy choice made by governments that tax the poor and subsidize the rich. It can be reversed by the same means: policy. A high-level UBI, funded by expropriating the excesses of the ultra-wealthy, is a declaration that every human being has inherent worth, independent of labor, independent of GDP, independent of the whims of capital markets.

There is no time for small steps. Automation is accelerating. Wealth concentration is worsening. The social fabric is tearing. We need a solution that matches the scale of the crisis: a universal basic income high enough to end poverty, funded by wealth taxes high enough to end oligarchy, and supported by monetary expansion bold enough to prioritize public need over private greed. Let the ships burn. Let the wealth be redistributed. Let every person, from birth to death, know that they are safe. This is not a utopian dream. A Universal Basic Income (UBI) set at a very high level—high enough to cover basic living costs, not just a token supplement—is a radical departure from current welfare states. Its supporters argue that, if paired with the right financing, it would transform society. Below are the main reasons and supposed benefits, with an emphasis on poverty, inequality, and automation.

1. Eliminating Poverty

The most direct goal is to end poverty by definition. If every person receives a monthly income above the poverty line, then no one falls below it, regardless of employment status, family breakdown, disability, or economic downturn.

  • Replaces the safety net with a floor: Unlike means-tested programs, UBI has no “cliffs” where a small pay rise causes a sudden loss of benefits. People can earn more without losing their basic income.
  • Reduces bureaucratic complexity: A universal payment could replace dozens of targeted programs, eliminating administrative costs and the humiliating paperwork often associated with poverty relief.
  • Prevents destitution even in crises: In recessions, pandemics, or personal emergencies, the income keeps arriving. There is no delay while applications are processed or eligibility is verified.

At a very high level, the effect is even stronger: it would not merely reduce poverty but effectively abolish absolute poverty in the country that adopts it.

2. Reducing Economic Inequality

Extremely progressive taxation—e.g., high marginal rates on top incomes, wealth taxes, inheritance taxes, and corporate taxes—would be used to fund the UBI. This creates a two-sided redistribution:

  • Cash to everyone: Those at the bottom receive a large income they did not earn, lifting them relative to the rest of society.
  • Surtaxes on the wealthy: Those at the top pay substantially more in taxes. Theafter-tax difference between the richest and poorest shrinks dramatically.

Supporters argue this would:

  • Reassert social equality: Extreme wealth concentration distorts politics, media, and opportunity. A high UBI funded by progressive taxation counters that concentration.
  • Increase social mobility: With a guaranteed decent income, people can afford education, training, relocation, or starting a business without fear of falling into homelessness.
  • Reduce status anxiety and crime: Some economists argue that inequality itself causes social harms—from poorer health to higher crime. A high UBI would mitigate those.

3. Providing Security in the Face of Automation-Related Unemployment

Automation, AI, and robotics are expected to displace millions of workers. Even if new jobs are created, they may require skills that displaced workers don’t have, and the transition could be severe.

  • Decouples survival from employment: In a world where labor is increasingly automated, UBI ensures people can survive even if there simply aren’t enough decent jobs to go around. It treats the profits from automation as a common dividend rather than a windfall for capital owners alone.
  • Reduces fear of technological change: If people know their basic needs are covered, they are less likely to resist automation or demand artificially protected jobs. Society can embrace productivity gains.
  • Supports gig and precarious work: Many future jobs may be short-term, freelancing, or project-based. UBI acts as a stable base, allowing workers to take on creative or part-time work without risking poverty.
  • Empowers workers in the labor market: With a guaranteed outside option, workers can refuse exploitative wages or dangerous conditions. This is sometimes called the “bargaining power effect”: UBI strengthens labor’s position, potentially raising wages for lower-paid work.

4. Supposed Broader Social Benefits

A high UBI is also expected to:

Supporters of a very high UBI often debate two financing methods:

A. Extremely Progressive Taxation

This means raising revenue by taxing the wealthy, large corporations, and capital gains at very high rates. Benefits:

  • Reduces inequality twice over: once by taking from the rich, once by giving to everyone.

B. Monetary Expansion

Some propose financing UBI by “printing money” or central bank digital money creation. Supposed benefits:

  • Avoids the need to tax many people directly.
  • Can be implemented quickly, especially in a crisis.
  • If the economy has spare capacity, new money boosts demand without causing inflation.

However, critics note that this is risky: if spending outpaces production, the result is inflation that erodes the real value of the UBI. Many supporters therefore prefer taxation or a combination of taxes and a carefully managed public money issuance tied to productive capacity.

While the reasons above are the core “supposed benefits,” any honest explanation should note the main objections:

  • Incentive effects: A very high UBI might discourage some paid work. Supporters respond that it also frees people to do better work, but the net effect is debated.
  • Cost is enormous: A high UBI would require historically unprecedented tax increases. It may be politically impossible, or it may drive capital and talent abroad.
  • Monetary financing is dangerous: Unchecked money creation can cause hyperinflation, especially if the supply side does not expand.
  • Not a cure for all structural problems: Housing shortages, healthcare costs, and discrimination remain. UBI gives people money, but it doesn’t build homes or fix monopolies.

Conclusion

The case for a very high UBI financed by extremely progressive taxation rests on a simple moral and economic vision: abundance should be shared. In an age of immense wealth and automation, no one should be left destitute simply because their labor is no longer needed. Supporters believe that replacing the “iron link between income and work” would eliminate poverty, shrink inequality, and give people the security and freedom to adapt to a rapidly changing economy. Whether that vision is realistic or desirable remains one of the most important economic debates of the 21st century.

A Case for Bold Redistribution in the Age of Unprecedented Wealth

To understand why moderate policy tinkering is insufficient, one must first confront the raw dimensions of the problem.

In the United States alone, approximately 37.9 million people live below the official poverty line — a threshold that most economists agree dramatically understates true material hardship.
