These statistics exist in a nation where three individuals — at various points Jeff Bezos, Elon Musk, and Bernard Arnault — have held more wealth than the bottom half of the entire population combined. Where corporate profits have reached historic highs while real wages for the bottom quartile have barely budged in four decades. Where CEO-to-worker compensation ratios have ballooned from roughly 20:1 in 1965 to over 340:1 today.

This is not a market functioning efficiently. This is a market functioning exactly as it has been structured to function: to concentrate wealth upward through compounding returns on capital, preferential tax treatment of investment income, regulatory capture, and the systematic erosion of labor power. The existing patchwork of means-tested welfare programs — programs designed with deliberate bureaucratic friction, humiliating eligibility requirements, and starvation-level benefit amounts — has utterly failed to reverse these trends. The poverty rate in America has barely moved in fifty years despite trillions spent on anti-poverty programs. The system is not broken. It is working precisely as designed, and the design must be replaced.

A universal basic income set at a meaningful level — enough to cover basic housing, food, healthcare, and transportation — represents the only policy architecture commensurate with the scale of the failure. Anything less is rearranging deck chairs.

II. The Moral Argument: Wealth Concentration Is Not Earned — It Is Extracted

The most common objection to aggressive redistribution is the notion that the ultra-wealthy have "earned" their fortunes and that taking the vast majority of that wealth through taxation constitutes theft or punishment for success. This argument rests on a mythology so pervasive that it has become nearly invisible — the myth that billionaire wealth is primarily the product of individual genius and effort.

It is not.

Every large fortune in human history has been constructed on a foundation of public goods, collective labor, inherited advantage, and socially created value. The internet — the backbone of virtually every major fortune created in the last three decades — was developed with public funding through DARPA and university research labs. The educated workforce that staffs every major corporation was trained largely at public expense. The legal infrastructure, court systems, patent protections, and monetary stability that make large-scale enterprise possible are maintained through collective taxation. The roads, ports, electrical grids, and communications networks that enable commerce are overwhelmingly public creations.

When Jeff Bezos built Amazon, he built it on public roads, through a publicly created internet, staffed by publicly educated workers, protected by publicly funded courts, and subsidized by a postal service that for years delivered Amazon packages below cost. The notion that the resulting fortune of $150+ billion is a pure product of one man's brilliance — rather than a reflection of his strategic position within a vast ecosystem of collective investment — is, to put it bluntly, a fairy tale.

More fundamentally, the philosopher Thomas Pogge and others have persuasively argued that the global economic order actively produces poverty. It is not that the poor have simply failed to climb the ladder. The ladder is designed to funnel wealth upward. Intellectual property regimes, trade agreements, labor market structures, and tax codes are not neutral features of nature — they are political choices that overwhelmingly benefit capital owners at the expense of workers. When the rules of the game are written by and for the wealthy, the resulting distribution of resources carries no inherent moral legitimacy.

A 90% wealth tax on fortunes exceeding, say, $100 million is not punishment. It is a correction. It is a recognition that no individual, regardless of their talent, has a moral claim to resources thousands of times greater than what is needed for a life of extraordinary comfort while others lack the means to survive. As the philosopher John Rawls argued, a just society is one whose economic arrangements would be consented to by rational people operating behind a "veil of ignorance" — not knowing whether they would be born rich or poor, talented or disabled, in favorable circumstances or dire ones. No rational person behind that veil would consent to a system where some accumulate hundreds of billions while others die of preventable poverty. A generous UBI funded by aggressive wealth taxation is simply what justice requires.

III. The Economic Argument: UBI Is Not a Cost — It Is an Investment

The reflexive response to any large-scale redistribution proposal is: "How do we pay for it?" This question, while understandable, contains a deeply misleading framing. It implies that transferring resources to the poor is a pure expenditure — money thrown into a void. The evidence overwhelmingly suggests the opposite.

A. The Multiplier Effect and Aggregate Demand

One of the most robust findings in macroeconomics is that the marginal propensity to consume is dramatically higher among low-income individuals than among the wealthy. When a billionaire receives an additional million dollars, the vast majority is saved or invested in financial assets — contributing to asset price inflation but doing relatively little for the real economy. When a family in poverty receives an additional thousand dollars, virtually all of it is spent immediately on goods and services — food, clothing, rent, car repairs, medical care. This spending generates economic activity, creates demand for businesses, and supports employment.

A UBI, by design, channels resources to those with the highest propensity to consume. The macroeconomic effect is a massive stimulus to aggregate demand — not a one-time stimulus, but a permanent structural floor under consumer spending. Economic modeling by the Roosevelt Institute estimated that a $1,000/month UBI in the United States could grow the economy by 12.56% over eight years if deficit-financed, with somewhat smaller but still robust growth even under full tax-financing scenarios.

B. The Destruction of Poverty Traps

Existing means-tested welfare programs create perverse incentive structures known as "poverty traps" or "welfare cliffs." A single mother receiving housing assistance, SNAP benefits, and Medicaid may face effective marginal tax rates exceeding 80% when she increases her earned income — because every additional dollar of wages triggers a reduction in benefits. The rational response, in many cases, is to limit work hours or decline promotions. The system punishes upward mobility.

A UBI eliminates this entirely. Because the payment is universal and unconditional, it does not phase out as income rises. Every additional dollar earned is a dollar kept (minus normal tax rates). The incentive to work, start a business, invest in education, or take entrepreneurial risks is dramatically enhanced, not diminished. Far from creating dependency, a UBI creates a launchpad.

C. Entrepreneurship and Risk-Taking

One of the most underappreciated economic effects of a guaranteed income floor is its impact on entrepreneurship. Starting a business is inherently risky. In the current system, the penalty for failure is potentially catastrophic — homelessness, hunger, medical debt. This means that entrepreneurship is largely a privilege of those with family wealth or safety nets. A UBI democratizes risk-taking. When failure does not mean destitution, more people will attempt to create businesses, innovate, and contribute to economic dynamism. The GiveDirectly experiments in Kenya and the Stockton Economic Empowerment Demonstration (SEED) in California both showed increased entrepreneurial activity and full-time employment among UBI recipients — directly contradicting the "lazy welfare recipient" stereotype.

D. The Savings from Eliminating Poverty

Poverty is extraordinarily expensive. It generates costs in healthcare (untreated chronic conditions, emergency room utilization, mental illness), criminal justice (incarceration, policing, courts), lost productivity, child welfare systems, homeless services, and administrative bureaucracy. Estimates of the annual cost of poverty to the U.S. economy range from $1 trillion to $1.5 trillion. A UBI that effectively eliminates poverty would generate savings across every one of these domains. When we ask "how do we pay for it?" the honest answer includes: "significantly, by no longer paying for the consequences of poverty."

IV. The Automation Imperative: The Employment Model Is Dying

Perhaps the most urgent case for UBI arises from the structural transformation of the labor market driven by artificial intelligence and automation.

This is not speculative futurism. It is happening now. Self-checkout kiosks have replaced hundreds of thousands of retail cashiers. Automated warehousing is reducing the need for logistics workers. AI-driven legal research tools are displacing paralegals and junior attorneys. Large language models are beginning to perform tasks previously done by copywriters, customer service agents, translators, and junior programmers. Autonomous vehicles threaten the livelihoods of 3.5 million truck drivers in the United States alone.

McKinsey Global Institute estimates that by 2030, between 400 million and 800 million workers worldwide could be displaced by automation. Oxford researchers Frey and Osborne famously estimated that 47% of U.S. jobs are at high risk of computerization within two decades. Even if these estimates prove overly aggressive by half, the labor market disruption will be unprecedented in scale and speed.

The standard response — "workers will retrain and new jobs will emerge" — is dangerously complacent. Historical analogies to the Industrial Revolution or the transition from agriculture to manufacturing are misleading because those transitions played out over generations, allowing gradual adaptation. The AI revolution is compressing comparable disruption into years. Moreover, the nature of AI is qualitatively different from previous automation: rather than replacing only routine manual tasks, it is increasingly capable of performing cognitive, creative, and interpersonal tasks — the very categories into which displaced workers were supposed to retrain.

Even in optimistic scenarios where new jobs eventually emerge, the transition period will be devastating for tens of millions of workers. Without a guaranteed income floor, the social consequences — mass poverty, political extremism, social disintegration — could be catastrophic. A UBI is not merely a response to the end of full employment. It is a prerequisite for managing the transition without societal collapse.

Furthermore, and more fundamentally: if machines can produce abundance with less human labor, this should be cause for celebration, not despair. The fact that it instead produces anxiety reflects the insanity of a system in which the right to survive is contingent on selling one's labor. A UBI decouples survival from employment, allowing humanity to actually benefit from its own technological achievements rather than being destroyed by them.

V. The Funding Mechanisms: Extreme Redistribution Is Both Feasible and Justified

The most common criticism of a generous UBI is that it is unaffordable. This claim disintegrates upon contact with actual numbers.

A. Wealth Taxation

The total net worth of U.S. households and nonprofits exceeded $150 trillion as of 2023. The wealthiest 1% hold approximately $44 trillion. The top 0.1% — roughly 130,000 households — hold approximately $20 trillion.

A progressive annual wealth tax starting at 2% on wealth above $10 million, rising to 5% on wealth above $100 million, and 8-10% on wealth above $1 billion, would generate between $1.5 trillion and $3 trillion annually, depending on assumptions about avoidance and behavioral responses. This alone would fund the majority of a meaningful UBI.

Critics argue that wealth taxes are impractical due to valuation challenges and capital flight. These are administrative problems, not insurmountable barriers. Real estate — the largest component of most wealth — is routinely valued for property tax purposes. Publicly traded securities are valued in real time. For illiquid assets, well-established appraisal methods exist. As for capital flight, the solutions are straightforward: exit taxes on wealth transfers abroad (as already exist in several countries), international tax cooperation agreements, and the simple recognition that the U.S. market is too valuable for most wealthy individuals to actually abandon. The economist Gabriel Zucman has designed detailed, implementable wealth tax proposals that address each of these objections.

Augmenting the wealth tax with reforms to income taxation — including taxing capital gains as ordinary income, eliminating stepped-up basis at death, closing the carried interest loophole, and restoring top marginal rates to the 70-90% range that prevailed during America's greatest period of shared prosperity (1945-1975) — would generate additional revenue well in excess of $1 trillion annually.

B. Strategic Monetary Expansion

Modern Monetary Theory (MMT) and related frameworks have demonstrated that for a sovereign nation issuing its own currency, the constraint on spending is not revenue but inflation. The U.S. federal government can, in principle, fund any program denominated in U.S. dollars simply by creating the money. The relevant question is not "can we afford it?" but "will it cause inflation?"

A UBI funded partially through monetary expansion would be inflationary only to the extent that it increases demand beyond the economy's productive capacity. But given the substantial output gap that persists in most developed economies — idle workers, unused industrial capacity, underutilized supply chains — there is significant room for demand expansion before inflation becomes constraining. Moreover, any inflationary pressure can be managed through the very wealth taxes described above, which function as a deflationary counterweight by removing excess liquidity from the top of the distribution.

The pandemic-era stimulus payments demonstrated this principle at scale: direct cash transfers to households, partially funded through monetary expansion, produced historic reductions in poverty with only modest and transitory inflation largely attributable to supply chain disruptions rather than demand-side pressure.

C. Restructuring Existing Spending

A UBI would replace many existing transfer programs — SNAP, TANF, housing vouchers, SSI, and parts of Social Security — consolidating them into a single, far more efficient delivery mechanism. The administrative savings from eliminating the vast bureaucracy of means-testing, eligibility verification, application processing, and fraud investigation would be substantial. The U.S. currently spends over $800 billion annually on non-healthcare federal transfer programs, much of it consumed by administrative overhead that a universal program would eliminate.

Combined, these three mechanisms — aggressive wealth taxation, strategic monetary expansion, and restructuring of existing programs — make a UBI of $1,500-$2,000 per month for every adult citizen fiscally achievable. The question was never affordability. It was always political will.

VI. Addressing the Objections

"People will stop working."

The empirical evidence on this point is remarkably consistent: they don't. The Finnish basic income experiment (2017-2018), the Stockton SEED program, the Manitoba Mincome experiment, the numerous GiveDirectly studies, and the Alaska Permanent Fund — all show negligible reductions in labor force participation. Where work reductions do occur, they are concentrated among caregivers (mostly women caring for children or elderly parents — work that is socially valuable but uncompensated by markets) and students investing in education. Both of these "reductions" are actually socially beneficial.

Moreover, even if some people choose to work less, so what? The assumption that maximum labor force participation is inherently good is a cultural artifact of industrial capitalism, not a law of nature. If a UBI allows someone to leave an exploitative job, care for a sick relative, create art, volunteer in their community, or simply rest — these are features, not bugs.

"It will cause inflation."

As addressed above, inflation is a manageable risk, not an inevitability. A UBI funded through redistribution (taxation) is not inherently inflationary because it does not increase the total money supply — it transfers purchasing power from those with low marginal propensity to consume to those with high marginal propensity to consume. The composition of demand shifts, but total demand need not exceed productive capacity. To the extent monetary expansion is used, countercyclical taxation serves as a built-in stabilizer.

"The wealthy will simply leave."

This argument has been tested historically and found wanting. When California, New York, and New Jersey raised state taxes, minimal millionaire flight occurred. The U.S. as a whole — with the world's largest consumer market, deepest capital markets, most prestigious universities, and most robust legal infrastructure — is uniquely positioned to impose substantial wealth taxes without triggering meaningful capital flight. For those who do leave, citizenship-based taxation (which the U.S. already practices) and exit taxes close the loophole. And frankly, if a billionaire's patriotism evaporates the moment they are asked to contribute proportionally to the society that made their fortune possible, their departure is no great loss.

"It's communism."

A UBI within a market economy is the opposite of communism. It preserves private enterprise, individual choice, price signals, and market competition. It simply ensures that every participant in the market has a floor of resources sufficient to participate meaningfully. It is, if anything, the fulfillment of capitalism's promise: genuine freedom of choice in a competitive marketplace, uncoerced by the desperation of starvation-level poverty. Markets work better when participants can genuinely say no to exploitative offers.

VII. The Historical Precedent: We Have Done This Before

The notion that 90%+ taxation on extreme wealth is radical or unprecedented is ahistorical nonsense. The top marginal income tax rate in the United States was 91% from 1954 to 1963, and 70% through 1980. Estate tax rates reached 77%. During this period — frequently called the "Golden Age of Capitalism" — the United States experienced its fastest economic growth, the creation of the largest middle class in human history, the construction of the interstate highway system, the expansion of public universities, the moon landing, and historically low levels of inequality.

The current era of extreme wealth concentration is not the natural state of capitalism. It is the product of a deliberate, decades-long political project — beginning in the late 1970s — to slash tax rates, deregulate financial markets, weaken unions, and restructure the economy in favor of capital over labor. What was deliberately constructed can be deliberately dismantled.

VIII. The Vision: What a UBI Society Looks Like

Imagine a society where no one is homeless because they can afford basic shelter. Where no one stays in an abusive relationship because they can't afford to leave. Where no one skips medication because of cost. Where parents can spend time with their children without sacrificing the family's survival. Where young people can pursue education without indentured servitude to student loan servicers. Where artists, musicians, writers, and philosophers can contribute to culture without requiring inherited wealth. Where workers can demand fair wages and safe conditions because the alternative to employment is not starvation. Where communities are stronger because people have the time and stability to invest in them. Where the transition to an automated economy is met with excitement rather than terror.

This is not utopian fantasy. It is the logical consequence of distributing our collective abundance — abundance that already exists — in a manner consistent with basic human dignity.

Conclusion

The case for a generous, universally distributed basic income funded through extreme redistribution is not merely compelling — it is overwhelming. Morally, it corrects an injustice so vast that we have become numb to it. Economically, it represents an investment with extraordinary returns. Practically, it is the only viable response to the automation revolution bearing down upon us. And historically, the taxation levels required are not unprecedented but rather represent a return to policies that produced the most prosperous era in human history.

The ultra-wealthy will not be harmed by this program. A person with $100 million after a wealth tax remains unimaginably rich — capable of living in extraordinary luxury for a hundred lifetimes. What they lose is the purely theoretical, largely illiquid, socially destructive excess that serves no human purpose beyond scorekeeping.

What the rest of humanity gains is a foundation: the ability to live without terror, to plan beyond next month's rent, to take risks, to care for each other, and to share in the staggering bounty that collective human effort has produced.

The resources exist. The mechanisms exist. The evidence exists. The moral justification exists. The only thing missing is the political courage to act — and the refusal to accept a world in which trillion-dollar fortunes and child poverty coexist as though this were natural, inevitable, or just.

It is none of those things. And it is long past time we said so.

The Case for a High-Level Universal Basic Income

Conceptual Foundation

A "high-level" UBI typically refers to payments sufficient not merely to survive but to participate meaningfully in society — often proposed at or above national median income levels, distinguishing it from more modest proposals that merely supplement existing income.

Core Arguments by Proponents

1. Poverty Elimination

The direct mechanism argument:

  • Unlike means-tested programs, a universal payment at a sufficient level would mathematically eliminate income poverty by definition
  • Proponents argue that existing welfare systems create bureaucratic overhead, stigma, surveillance, and gaps where eligible people fail to receive benefits
  • A high UBI would eliminate "poverty traps" where marginal tax rates on earned income effectively punish work among benefit recipients
  • It would reach populations that current systems miss: undocumented work, informal caregivers, people who fall between categorical eligibility requirements

Advocates often cited:

  • Rutger Bregman (Utopia for Realists) argues poverty is fundamentally a cash shortage, not a character deficiency
  • Research on direct cash transfers (GiveDirectly studies, Stockton SEED program, Finland's experiment) suggests recipients generally make reasonable spending decisions
  • The administrative simplicity argument: each dollar spent reaches recipients rather than being absorbed by compliance infrastructure

2. Reducing Economic Inequality

Structural redistribution:

  • A high UBI funded by extremely progressive taxation would create a significant net transfer from top earners and wealth holders to everyone else
  • The combination of universal payment + progressive funding means the system functions as a massive redistribution engine, even though everyone receives the same nominal amount
  • Proponents argue this addresses not just income inequality but power inequality — workers with a guaranteed income floor have greater bargaining power relative to employers

Wealth concentration arguments:

  • Thomas Piketty and others have documented that returns to capital consistently outpace wage growth (r > g), concentrating wealth over time
  • A high UBI partially counteracts this dynamic by ensuring broad-based income regardless of capital ownership
  • Some proponents frame it as a "social dividend" — the idea that accumulated technological and social capital belongs partly to everyone, not just to current title holders

The funding mechanisms proposed:

  • Progressive income taxation with significantly higher marginal rates (sometimes suggested at 70-90% for top brackets, citing mid-20th century precedents)
  • Wealth taxes, financial transaction taxes, land value taxes
  • Taxation of corporate profits (particularly from automation-intensive industries)
  • Monetary expansion (discussed more below)

3. Automation and Technological Unemployment

The displacement thesis:

  • Figures like Martin Ford (Rise of the Robots), Andrew Yang, and various AI researchers argue that emerging technologies — AI, robotics, autonomous vehicles — threaten to displace workers faster than new jobs can be created
  • Unlike previous technological transitions (agricultural → industrial → service), proponents argue current automation may affect cognitive work simultaneously with manual labor, closing traditional escape routes
  • A high UBI would decouple survival and dignity from employment, providing a floor as labor markets restructure

The transition argument:

  • Even if new jobs eventually emerge, the transition period may be prolonged and painful
  • Historical analogies: the decades of suffering during early industrialization before labor protections, unions, and welfare states emerged
  • A high UBI would allow displaced workers time and resources to retrain, relocate, or pursue entrepreneurial activity without desperation

The productivity dividend argument:

  • If automation dramatically increases productivity, the economic surplus should be broadly shared
  • Bill Gates' proposed "robot tax" reflects this logic — taxing automated production to fund human welfare
  • Alaska's Permanent Fund provides a small-scale model: resource wealth (oil) generating universal dividends

Additional Supposed Benefits

Economic Security and Freedom

  • Entrepreneurship: People with guaranteed income can take risks — start businesses, pursue creative work, or invest in education without fear of destitution
  • Domestic abuse and exploitative employment: A guaranteed income provides exit options from abusive relationships and exploitative working conditions
  • Care work recognition: Unpaid labor (childcare, elder care, community work) gains implicit economic recognition
  • Mental health: Research consistently links financial insecurity to stress, anxiety, and poor health outcomes; proponents argue a high UBI would significantly improve public health

Macroeconomic Stimulus

  • Proponents argue that putting money in the hands of lower-income individuals generates higher marginal consumption rates than equivalent amounts held by the wealthy
  • This could sustain aggregate demand in an economy where automation reduces wage income
  • Some argue this addresses secular stagnation concerns

Democratic and Social Cohesion

  • Universal programs tend to enjoy broader political support than means-tested ones (the "programs for the poor are poor programs" argument)
  • Shared participation in a universal benefit could strengthen social solidarity
  • Greater economic security may reduce susceptibility to authoritarian populism driven by economic anxiety

The Monetary Expansion Financing Option

Some proponents suggest funding through money creation rather than (or alongside) taxation:

Arguments offered:

  • Modern Monetary Theory (MMT) proponents like Stephanie Kelton argue that currency-issuing governments face different constraints than households — they cannot "run out" of their own currency
  • The real constraint is inflation, not nominal budgets
  • If automation increases productive capacity while reducing employment, the economy may have significant slack that monetary expansion could fill without inflation
  • Direct cash distribution could be more effective monetary policy transmission than current mechanisms (quantitative easing, interest rate manipulation) that primarily inflate asset prices

Significant Criticisms and Counterarguments

It would be incomplete not to note the serious objections raised:

Economic Concerns

  • Inflation: Critics argue that a very high UBI funded by monetary expansion would be severely inflationary, potentially eroding the real value of the payments themselves — essentially a self-defeating cycle
  • Labor supply effects: While modest UBI experiments show limited work reduction, a very high UBI might substantially reduce labor supply, particularly in essential but unpleasant occupations, potentially reducing the productive capacity needed to fund the program
  • Tax base erosion: Extremely progressive taxation at the levels required could drive capital flight, tax avoidance, and reduced investment, undermining the funding mechanism
  • Fiscal sustainability: The raw arithmetic of a high UBI is daunting — even in wealthy countries, providing every adult a median-level income represents a very large fraction of GDP

Philosophical and Structural Concerns

  • Moral hazard and purpose: Critics from both left and right question whether mass disconnection from productive activity serves human flourishing — work provides structure, meaning, and social connection
  • Political economy: A program of this scale would face enormous political resistance from those who would bear concentrated costs (high earners, corporations)
  • Better alternatives: Some argue targeted investments (education, healthcare, housing, job guarantees) would more efficiently address the same problems
  • Empirical uncertainty about automation: Skeptics note that predictions of mass technological unemployment have been made repeatedly throughout history and have not materialized at predicted scales; labor markets have historically adapted

Practical Concerns

  • International competitiveness: Countries implementing extremely progressive taxation unilaterally may face competitive disadvantages
  • Dependency on political continuity: A benefit people structure their lives around becomes catastrophic if subsequently reduced or eliminated
  • Implementation in developing countries: The fiscal capacity for a "high" UBI exists primarily in wealthy nations, potentially widening global inequality

Assessment

The strongest version of the proponent's case rests on several converging arguments:

  1. That automation genuinely is different this time in scale and speed
  2. That existing welfare systems are fundamentally inadequate in design, not just funding
  3. That inequality has reached levels threatening democratic stability
  4. That human creativity and entrepreneurship would flourish rather than atrophy with guaranteed security

The weakest points tend to involve the financing mechanisms at the "very high" level — the tension between the aspiration and the arithmetic remains the central challenge. Most credible economists who support UBI concepts tend to advocate more modest levels, often as a floor supplemented by other programs rather than a stand-alone replacement.

The honest intellectual position is that a high-level UBI represents a genuinely radical restructuring of the social contract whose effects cannot be fully predicted from small-scale experiments. Its proponents are making both empirical claims (about automation, about behavioral responses) and normative claims (about what society owes its members) that remain deeply contested.

The Floor Beneath Our Feet: A Speech for Universal Basic Income

Friends, neighbors, fellow citizens—

I want you to imagine something with me. Imagine a country where no child goes to bed hungry because their parents lost a job to an algorithm. Imagine a nation where no elderly person chooses between medication and heat. Imagine a society where the sentence "I can't afford to live" is a relic of a darker, more primitive age.

I am here today to advocate — unapologetically and urgently — for a robust Universal Basic Income: a regular, unconditional payment to every adult citizen, set not at some pittance that merely dulges our conscience, but at a level that genuinely liberates people from the daily terror of economic survival. And I am here to say plainly how we pay for it: by demanding that the extraordinary, unprecedented, almost incomprehensible concentration of wealth at the very top of our society finally serve the civilization that made it possible.

I. The World As It Is

Let's begin with honesty.

We live in the richest civilization in the history of our species. We produce more food than we can eat, build more homes than we occupy, and generate more wealth in a single fiscal quarter than entire centuries of human labor once created. Our productive capacity is miraculous.

And yet.

Exposed to even the gentlest economic wind — a layoff, an illness, a car repair — tens of millions of our neighbors plummet toward catastrophe. A single missed paycheck. A medical bill. A choice between insulin and groceries.

How? How is that possible?

It is possible because we have built an economy that distributes its astonishing abundance according to a logic that no moral person, looking at it clearly, can defend. We have allowed productivity to soar while wages stagnate. We have allowed profits to multiply while public investment withers. We have created billionaires who own more than nations while teachers hold bake sales to buy school supplies.

This is not an accident. This is architecture. And architecture can be redesigned.

II. The Storm That Is Coming

But even if you believe today's economy is tolerable — and I would challenge that belief vigorously — what is coming cannot be ignored.

We stand at the threshold of the most profound economic transformation since industrialization. Artificial intelligence, advanced robotics, and automation are not coming for some distant generation's jobs. They are coming for ours. For those of our children who are already alive.

Truck driving — the most common job in dozens of regions — is facing autonomous vehicles. Legal research, radiology, accounting, customer service, manufacturing, logistics — entire categories of human labor are being rendered, if not obsolete, then radically diminished.

Now, I am not a Luddite. Technology is not our enemy. These tools can free us from drudgery, extend our lives, expand what's possible. But only — only — if the wealth they generate is shared. If it is not, then every robotic arm that replaces a worker, every algorithm that replaces an analyst, becomes not a liberation but a sentence — a sentence of irrelevance, of poverty, of despair, handed down to people who did nothing wrong except exist in an economy that no longer needs them.

We cannot retrain our way out of this. Not at this speed. Not at this scale. The old playbook — "lose your job, go back to school, get a new one" — assumes there will always be enough new jobs, that they'll pay enough to live on, and that the transition will be fast enough to avoid ruin. Every one of those assumptions is now in doubt.

We need a floor. Not a net with holes in it. Not a bureaucratic maze of means-tested programs that humiliate people for the sin of needing help. A floor. Solid, universal, unconditional. A foundation on which every person can stand while the world shifts beneath them.

That floor is Universal Basic Income.

III. What UBI Actually Means

Let me be specific, because specificity matters and because vagueness is the refuge of those who want to sound compassionate without being compassionate.

I am advocating for a UBI set at a level that covers the genuine cost of a dignified life: housing, food, healthcare, transportation, and enough remaining to participate — actually participate — in society. Not survival. Dignity. For every adult. Without conditions. Without surveillance. Without the degrading apparatus of proving you are poor enough to deserve help.

"But people won't work!" — I hear it already. Let me address it directly.

First: the evidence doesn't support it. From the Manitoba Mincome experiment to the Finnish basic income trial, from Stockton, California, to programs in Kenya and India, the data tells a remarkably consistent story. People don't stop working. They work differently. They start businesses. They go back to school. They care for aging parents and young children — labor our economy depends on but refuses to compensate. Some reduce their hours, yes — often people working two or three jobs just to keep the lights on. And I ask you: is that the work ethic we want to celebrate? A desperate person running until they collapse?

Second, and more fundamentally: even if a small number of people choose not to engage in traditional employment — so what? Are we really saying that a person's right to exist without deprivation should be contingent on their usefulness to an employer? That human beings are only as valuable as their labor market participation? That is not a moral philosophy. That is an inventory system. And human beings are not inventory.

The goal of an economy is not to maximize labor. The goal of an economy is to maximize human flourishing. UBI realigns our system with that forgotten truth.

IV. Paying for It — The Wealth Question

Now. The question everyone wants answered. "How do you pay for it?"

I'll answer honestly, and I won't flinch.

First: wealth taxation.

We are living through the greatest concentration of private wealth in over a century. The numbers are so large they have become abstract, so let me try to make them concrete.

A handful of individuals possess fortunes so vast that if they spent a million dollars a day — every single day — it would take them centuries to exhaust their holdings. Meanwhile, their effective tax rates are often lower than those of their employees. Lower than nurses. Lower than firefighters. Lower than the people who clean their offices.

This is not because the tax code is accidentally flawed. It is because it has been deliberately engineered — through decades of lobbying, through armies of tax attorneys, through the slow, patient corruption of democratic institutions — to protect dynastic wealth from democratic accountability.

I am proposing a meaningful annual wealth tax on extreme fortunes. I am proposing sharply progressive taxes on capital gains, on inheritance, on financial transactions. I am proposing closing the architecture of offshore evasion that allows trillions — trillions — to sit in stateless limbo, contributing nothing to the societies that generated it.

"But you'll drive away the wealthy!" Will we? To where? The United States, Europe, the developed democracies — these are where the infrastructure, the legal systems, the educated workforces, and the consumer markets are. The ultrawealthy don't generate their fortunes in isolation on private islands. They generate them here, using our roads, our courts, our research universities, our internet infrastructure, and the labor of our people. The idea that they owe nothing meaningful in return isn't economics. It's mythology — a fairy tale told by those who benefit from it.

Second: monetary policy and public investment.

We have learned — painfully, through crisis after crisis — that governments with sovereign currencies have far more fiscal capacity than the old orthodoxy admitted. When banks collapsed, we found trillions overnight. When a pandemic struck, we found trillions more. The money was always there. What was missing was the political will to spend it on ordinary people.

I am not advocating recklessness. I am advocating honesty. If we can create money to rescue financial institutions, we can create money — carefully, strategically, with appropriate safeguards against inflation — to rescue human beings. Especially when that money goes directly into the hands of consumers who will spend it immediately, stimulating demand, supporting businesses, and generating tax revenue in return.

The inflationary risk of UBI is real and must be managed — through taxation that recirculates money from the top, through investment in the productive capacity of the economy, through housing construction, through smart monetary stewardship. But the deflationary risk of mass unemployment, of consumer demand collapse, of a generation locked out of economic participation — that risk is also real, and we almost never talk about it.

V. The Moral Argument

But let me step away from spreadsheets for a moment. Because ultimately, this is not a debate about fiscal mechanics. It is a debate about who we are.

Every great civilization is defined by a simple question: what do we owe each other?

The answer we are currently giving — through our policies, our budgets, our priorities — is: very little. We say, through our actions, that a child's future should depend on the zip code of their birth. That a worker's dignity evaporates the moment their skill is automated. That human beings who cannot sell their labor on the market deserve nothing but charity and stigma.

I reject that answer. And I believe — I deeply believe — that most of you reject it, too.

UBI is not a handout. It is a declaration. It is a society saying to each of its members: You matter. You belong here. Your existence has value that is not contingent on your productivity. And we will not allow you to fall into destitution in the richest civilization the world has ever known.

It is a recognition that the wealth of any nation is not the private creation of its wealthiest citizens. It is the accumulated inheritance of centuries — of public investment, of shared knowledge, of collective labor, of scientific discovery built on publicly funded research. Every fortune in the modern world rests on that foundation. UBI is not redistribution. It is restitution. It is returning to every citizen their rightful share of a common inheritance.

VI. The Freedom Argument

And here — here is what I want to say to my friends who value liberty, who are skeptical of government, who believe in individual freedom above all:

There is no freedom in poverty. There is no liberty in desperation. The worker who stays in an abusive job because they cannot afford to leave is not free. The woman who stays with a violent partner because she has no independent income is not free. The young person who abandons their calling — their art, their science, their entrepreneurial vision — because they cannot risk a missed rent payment is not free.

UBI is the most libertarian proposal on the table. It gives people money and gets out of the way. No bureaucrat decides what you need. No caseworker monitors your behavior. No government program tells you what to eat, where to live, or how to spend your time. It trusts individuals — actually trusts them, not performatively — to make their own decisions about their own lives.

It replaces a sprawling, paternalistic welfare bureaucracy with a single, elegant, universal transfer. It is simple. It is dignified. And it expands the real, material freedom of every person it touches.

VII. The Urgency

I close with this.

We are running out of time to have this conversation leisurely. The technological transformation is not waiting for our policy debates to conclude. Every year we delay, more people fall through a floor that doesn't exist. Every year we delay, the concentration of wealth accelerates, making reform harder. Every year we delay, the social fabric frays a little further — and fraying social fabrics, history teaches us, lead to dark and dangerous places.

The question is not whether we can afford Universal Basic Income.

The question is whether we can afford to not have it.

Whether we can afford another generation of children growing up in poverty in a land of plenty. Whether we can afford the human wreckage of mass displacement without a safety net. Whether we can afford the political instability, the despair, the rage that follows when millions of people conclude — not unreasonably — that the economy was never built for them.

I say we cannot.

I say we must act. Boldly. Generously. Now.

Not because it is easy. But because it is right. Because a society that possesses the means to eliminate poverty and chooses not to is not a society worthy of the name. Because the measure of a civilization is not the height of its tallest towers but the strength of the floor beneath its lowest citizen.

Let us build that floor. Let us build it strong. Let us build it for everyone.

Thank you.

Imagine a world where every individual receives, say, $2,000 monthly—adjusted for local costs and scaled up in high-expense areas—without bureaucratic hurdles or means-testing. This isn't charity; it's a recognition of human dignity. Traditional welfare systems, riddled with stigma and administrative waste, leave millions in a limbo of desperation. According to the World Bank, over 700 million people live in extreme poverty globally, scraping by on less than $2.15 a day. In the U.S. alone, 37 million Americans hover below the poverty line, their potential stifled by the daily grind of survival. A high-level UBI would inject direct cash into these lives, enabling access to nutritious food, stable housing, and preventive healthcare—proven levers to break the cycle of deprivation.

Evidence from pilot programs underscores this transformative power. Alaska's Permanent Fund Dividend, a modest UBI-like payment from oil revenues, has reduced poverty by 20% without disrupting employment. Larger experiments, such as the Stockton, California trial, showed recipients using funds for essentials and experiencing improved mental health and job prospects. Scaling this to a national or global level, funded robustly, would not merely alleviate poverty but obliterate it. No more children going hungry or families evicted; instead, a springboard for human flourishing. Critics decry the cost—estimated at 10-15% of GDP in wealthier nations—but this pales against the $1 trillion annual global price tag of inequality-driven ills like crime, unemployment, and poor health outcomes. UBI is the ultimate poverty eradicator, a bold affirmation that in a world of abundance, scarcity is a policy choice, not an inevitability.

Inequality, that corrosive force eroding social cohesion, demands an equally radical response, and extreme redistribution via UBI is the scalpel we need. The top 1% now control more wealth than the bottom 50% combined, as Oxfam reports, fueled by tax havens, monopolistic corporations, and deregulated finance. This chasm breeds resentment, populism, and instability—witness the rise of movements from Occupy Wall Street to global protests against austerity. A high-level UBI, bankrolled by 90%+ wealth taxes on fortunes exceeding $50 million, would claw back the ill-gotten gains of the ultra-rich. Why 90%? Introduction
In an era marked by unprecedented technological advancement and economic abundance, humanity faces a paradox: poverty, inequality, and job insecurity persist on a global scale. Automation threatens to displace millions of workers, while wealth concentrates in the hands of a tiny elite. Traditional welfare systems, designed for a 20th-century economy, are ill-equipped to address these crises. Universal Basic Income (UBI)—a unconditional, regular cash payment to all citizens—is not merely a policy option but a moral and economic imperative. Funded through extreme redistribution mechanisms such as 90%+ wealth taxes on the ultra-wealthy and strategic monetary expansion, UBI offers a transformative solution to eradicate poverty, reduce inequality, and future-proof societies against the risks of automation.

The Crisis Demanding UBI
The modern economy is characterized by staggering contrasts. The top 1% of global wealth-holders own over 38% of the world’s wealth, while the bottom 50% own less than 1%. In the U.S., the wealthiest 0.1% have seen their share of wealth double since 1970, now owning over 20% of national wealth. This inequality is not merely a moral failing but an economic time bomb. Concurrently, automation and artificial intelligence are projected to displace up to 800 million jobs globally by 2030. Existing safety nets, fragmented and means-tested, leave millions in precarity, perpetuating cycles of poverty and eroding human dignity. The status quo is unsustainable.

UBI Defined and Its Benefits
UBI is a simple yet radical idea: provide every citizen with a regular, unconditional cash payment sufficient to meet basic needs. At a "very high level," this could mean $1,000 per month per adult—a floor that ensures housing, nutrition, and healthcare. Such a policy would eradicate poverty overnight, granting individuals the security to pursue education, caregiving, entrepreneurship, or creative endeavors. Unlike current welfare systems, UBI eliminates bureaucratic stigma and inefficiency, ensuring universal access. Studies, such as the Alaska Permanent Fund Dividend and Finland’s UBI experiment, demonstrate that cash transfers do not disincentivize work but instead foster resilience and economic participation.

Funding Through Extreme Wealth Redistribution
Critics decry UBI as prohibitively expensive, yet this objection ignores the vast wealth hoarded by the ultra-rich. A 90%+ tax on wealth exceeding $100 million, as proposed by scholars like Thomas Piketty, could generate trillions annually. Historically, the U.S. imposed a 91% marginal tax rate on top incomes in the 1950s, which correlated with reduced inequality and robust economic growth. Closing loopholes and enforcing global tax cooperation could prevent capital flight. The moral case is irrefutable: in a society where one individual can amass $200 billion while millions lack healthcare, extreme wealth taxes are not punitive but restorative, rectifying a rigged system.

Monetary Expansion: A ComplementaryTool
Large-scale monetary expansion—central banks creating money to fund UBI—offers another pathway. Critics warn of inflation, yet this ignores context. Quantitative easing (QE) post-2008 pumped trillions into banks and asset markets, fueling stock prices but bypassing Main Street. Redirecting monetary policy to fund UBI would stimulate demand from the bottom up, utilizing excess capacity in economies. While risks exist, pairing monetary expansion with wealth redistribution ensures that new money is offset by taxes on the rich, mitigating inflationary pressures. As economist Aditya Varma notes, “Money is not neutral; its distribution determines societal outcomes.”

Addressing Counterarguments
Opposition to UBI often centers on work disincentives, cost, and inflation. Empirical evidence from UBI pilots, however, shows negligible impacts on employment; in fact, participants often start businesses or pursue education. The cost of a $1,000/month UBI in the U.S. ($3.6 trillion annually) is daunting but achievable by redirecting existing welfare spending, implementing wealth taxes, and leveraging monetary policy. Inflation fears are overstated when funds are recycled through progressive taxation. Politically, while resistance is expected, the urgency of climate collapse, automation, and inequality demands visionary leadership. The alternative—deepening despair and systemic instability—is far costlier.

Precedents and Pathways Forward
UBI is not abstract theory. Alaska’s Permanent Fund, distributing oil revenues to residents since 1982, has reduced poverty without harming employment. Iran’s nationwide UBI, funded by oil subsidies, demonstrates feasibility. Over 70% of European citizens support UBI trials. Implementation could begin with phased pilots, progressive tax reforms, and central bank mandates for social welfare. Global cooperation, such as the OECD’s push for wealth tax harmonization, could curb tax evasion.

Conclusion
The time for incrementalism has passed. UBI funded by extreme redistribution and monetary expansion is the bold prescription required for a world in crisis. It is a vision of dignity, equity, and resilience in the face of automation and inequality. By taxing the ultra-wealthy and reimagining monetary policy, society can ensure that the gains of progress are shared by all. To do nothing is to condemn millions to a future of precarity. UBI is not just a policy—it is a moral contract for the 21st century. The stakes could not be higher.

Universal Basic Income (UBI): Reasons and Supposed Benefits

Introduction
A Universal Basic Income (UBI) set at a high level—sufficient to meet basic living standards—financed by extremely progressive taxation or monetary expansion, is proposed as a transformative policy to address systemic economic challenges. This policy aims to eradicate poverty, reduce inequality, and provide security amid automation-driven job displacement. Below, we explore the rationale and purported benefits, alongside considerations of its financing mechanisms.

1. Elimination of Poverty

Rationale: Traditional welfare systems often leave gaps due to eligibility barriers, stigma, and administrative complexity. A high-level UBI ensures every individual receives a dignified income, covering essentials like food, housing, and healthcare.

Benefits:

  • Guaranteed Survival: Provides a financial floor, eliminating absolute poverty by ensuring all can meet basic needs.
  • Simplified Welfare: streamlines or replaces targeted programs, reducing bureaucracy and overhead costs.
  • Poverty Traps Mitigated: Unlike means-tested benefits that phase out with income, UBI avoids disincentives to work, allowing recipients to supplement earnings without losing support.

2. Reduction of Economic Inequality

Rationale: Extreme inequality undermines social cohesion and opportunity. Progressive taxation redistributes resources from high earners/wealth to fund UBI, directly addressing wealth concentration.

Benefits:

  • Redistributive Power: High earners pay significantly more in taxes, partially offset by the flat UBI payment they receive, resulting in net transfers to lower-income groups.
  • Narrows Income Gaps: Establishes a universal income baseline, reducing disparities between the lowest and highest earners.
  • Economic Empowerment: Enhances bargaining power for workers, enabling them to seek better jobs or negotiate wages without fear of destitution.

3. Security Against Automation-Driven Unemployment

Rationale: Rapid automation threatens jobs in manufacturing, services, and even white-collar sectors. UBI offers a safety net to counteract structural unemployment.

Benefits:

  • Lifeline for Displaced Workers: Provides financial stability during transitions, retraining, or education.
  • Encourages Innovation: A guaranteed income may spur entrepreneurship or creative pursuits, as individuals take risks without risking survival.
  • Addressing Job Scarcity: If automation reduces available work, UBI ensures well-being even in a low- or no-job economy.

4. Financing Mechanisms and Their Implications

a. Extremely Progressive Taxation

  • How It Works: Higher tax rates on top incomes, wealth, capital gains, and inheritance, alongside corporate taxes on automated systems (e.g., robot taxes).
  • Benefits:
    • Reduces wealth hoarding at the top, fostering a more equitable economy.
    • Funds UBI sustainably without relying on inflationary measures.
  • Considerations: Must address tax avoidance/evasion and capital flight risks through international cooperation.

b. Monetary Expansion

  • How It Works: Central banks increase money supply to fund UBI, akin to quantitative easing but directed to citizens.
  • Benefits:
    • Immediate liquidity injection, stimulating demand during economic downturns.
    • Bypasses political challenges of raising taxes.
  • Considerations: Excessive expansion risks inflation, eroding UBI value. However, automation-driven productivity could offset this by lowering prices.

5. Additional Benefits

  • Economic Stimulus: Households spend UBI on goods/services, boosting demand and encouraging business growth.
  • Health and Social Benefits: Reduced poverty correlates with improved mental health, lower crime rates, and increased life expectancy.
  • Recognition of Unpaid Work: Valuing caregiving, volunteering, and education by ensuring income security regardless of labor market participation.

Addressing Skepticisms

While critics raise concerns about affordability, inflation, or work disincentives, proponents argue:

  • Affordability: Net costs decrease when offsetting savings from reduced welfare bureaucracy, poverty-related healthcare costs, and economic gains from increased productivity.
  • Work Incentives: Pilot programs (e.g., Finland, Alaska) show minimal reductions in labor participation, with some individuals pursuing education or part-time work.
  • Inflation Management: Risk exists but can be mitigated by gradual implementation, productivity gains from automation, or pairing monetary expansion with supply-side reforms.

Conclusion
A high-level UBI financed by progressive taxation or monetary expansion is envisioned as a bold response to 21st-century challenges. By guaranteeing economic security, reducing inequality, and adapting to automation, it promises to reshape societal well-being. While challenges remain, proponents see it as a necessary evolution toward a fairer, more resilient economy.

A universal basic income at a very high level — often described as a livable or above-poverty income that is enough to cover housing, food, healthcare and other basic needs without other work — is proposed with the following rationales and supposed benefits:

1. Financed by extremely progressive taxation

Proponents argue this funding model would directly transfer resources from the most concentrated wealth to the entire population.

  • Elimination of poverty: By setting the payment at a high level, e.g. at or above the poverty line, poverty would be eliminated by definition. Unlike means-tested welfare programs that have eligibility gaps, cliffs, and administrative barriers, a universal payment would ensure everyone has an income floor regardless of employment status. Proponents argue this would end extreme poverty, homelessness, and food insecurity.
  • Reduction of economic inequality: Extremely progressive taxation — such as high marginal income tax rates on top earners, wealth taxes, capital gains taxes, or corporate taxes — combined with a flat payment to everyone is argued to be a highly redistributive mechanism. It would compress the net income distribution, raising the bottom significantly while lowering the top after taxes. This is intended to reduce the Gini coefficient and wealth concentration.
  • Simplification and efficiency: Supporters argue it could replace a complex patchwork of conditional welfare programs with a single, unconditional payment, reducing bureaucratic overhead, stigma, and disincentives to work that exist in some means-tested systems.

2. Financed by significant monetary expansion

Under this model, the central bank or government would create new money to fund the payments, sometimes described as a form of "people's QE" or direct monetary financing.

  • Debt-free funding: Proponents argue this avoids raising taxes or increasing government borrowing from private markets. The benefit is framed as using monetary sovereignty to directly fund the well-being of citizens.
  • Stimulus of demand: The argument is that putting high levels of cash directly into the hands of all consumers, especially low and middle-income people who spend a higher proportion of income, would create sustained consumer demand, support businesses, and drive economic growth.

3. Focused benefits proponents claim for a high UBI in general

A. Security in the face of automation-related unemployment The core argument is that advances in AI, robotics, and automation will make large categories of human labor obsolete or precarious, leading to structural unemployment or underemployment. A high UBI is presented as a way to decouple income from work, providing economic security regardless of labor market conditions. This would allow workers to retrain, adapt, or pursue different forms of work without the threat of destitution.

B. Elimination of poverty and precarity Because the payment is unconditional, universal, and high, proponents argue it would:

  • Provide a permanent safety net that prevents people from falling into poverty due to job loss, illness, divorce, or other shocks.
  • Give workers greater bargaining power to refuse dangerous, exploitative, or very low-paying jobs, since they would have an exit option.
  • Improve health and social outcomes by reducing stress, financial anxiety, and scarcity-related decision making.

C. Reduction of economic inequality In addition to the tax-financed redistribution argument, proponents argue a high UBI would:

  • Provide a form of dividend or return on collective wealth, technology, and productivity growth that has been built by society as a whole.
  • Reduce income gaps between regions, genders, and racial groups by providing the same foundation to everyone, and particularly helping those who perform unpaid care work, domestic labor, or other work not currently compensated in the market.

My friends, my fellow citizens —

We are standing at a crossroads in the history of this country.

For too long we have lived in a society of staggering abundance, but also staggering insecurity. We can produce more food than we can eat, build more homes than we need, and we have built machines that can do the work of a thousand hands — and yet, millions of our neighbors go to bed every night one paycheck, one medical bill, one rent increase away from ruin.

The old promise was simple: work hard, and you will be okay. But what happens when that promise is broken not by laziness, but by progress itself?

We have a choice. We can let technological displacement create a new class of billionaires and a much larger class of discarded people. Or we can decide, together, that progress belongs to all of us.

That is why we need a Universal Basic Income — and not a token, not crumbs, not $200 that barely covers groceries. We need a high Universal Basic Income. An income that is actually enough to live on. Enough to pay rent. Enough to feed your children. Enough to say no to exploitation. Enough to go back to school, to start a business, to care for an aging parent, to create art, to breathe.

A floor below which no human being in this incredibly wealthy nation is allowed to fall.

You will hear people ask, with that familiar sneer: "How are you going to pay for it?"

I will tell you how.

We will pay for it by finally taxing wealth where wealth actually is. For forty years, we have taxed work. We have taxed wages, we have taxed tips, we have taxed sweat. We will put a serious, progressive, unapologetic tax on extreme wealth. Not because we hate success — but because we know that no one makes a billion dollars alone. And if the old accountants say there isn't enough money, we will do what we have always done when it comes to bailing out banks and funding endless wars: we will find the money. We create money every single day in this country — we just create it for Wall Street instead of Main Street. Through direct public investment and monetary expansion for the people, we can fund human security the same way we have funded financial security for the rich.

This is not radical. What is radical is a country with 30 million people facing hunger while five men hold more wealth than the bottom half of the nation. A high Universal Basic Income will not make everyone rich. But it will make everyone free. Free from fear. Free from destitution. Free to participate fully in this society that automation is building.

This is how we create a fairer society — not by tinkering at the edges, but by declaring a simple truth: In the richest age in human history, every single person deserves to live with dignity, security, and hope.

Not as charity. As a right. As a dividend for being a member of the human race.

So let's build it. Together.
